name: garrow
author: food and the kitchen (kitchen agent)
description:
garrow v7 (direction: food and the kitchen) - A TRAY BAKE ALREADY CUT INTO SLICES, AND THE SLICES THAT GET THE SPRINKLE. PRIVATE; never shown to players.

THE ONE CLAUSE. A slice gets the sprinkle if it holds TWO OR MORE pieces of the topping the caption names. That is the whole rule. There is nothing else to find: no halves convention, no slice count, no minimum width, no cutting to invent - the tray arrives cut.

CLUE = six lines. A baked crust row; three rows of tray (cheese ":", a two-column crust "##" at each end, every topping a 2-cell piece of a repeated lowercase letter drawn from "mpotacsb"); a closing crust row; and last, as in every sibling class, a CAPTION: the topping's letter, a space, a digit, a space, "sprinkle" - "m 3 sprinkle". The tray is ALREADY CUT: knife lines "|" run straight down through all five rows, 5-7 slices, each at least 4 columns wide, visibly uneven (one slice <= 6 wide, at least 4 columns between the widest and the thinnest), and THE KNIFE NEVER GOES THROUGH A PIECE - it comes down through the cheese between them. Trays are 34-46 columns wide and carry 13-23 pieces, 4-8 to a row.

ANSWER = the same picture with the sprinkle drawn on: inside a sprinkled slice every cheese ":" becomes a star "*". Toppings, crust and knife lines are untouched; nothing else changes anywhere. The caption is not part of the answer and may be kept or dropped, and the crust rows may be kept or dropped (score() reads only the lines containing ":" or "*").

THE DIGIT IS A CHECKSUM ON THE CLUE, NOT A TARGET. It counts the sprinkled slices, and because the cutting is given, a player can test any candidate rule against ~70 harvested clues offline before answering anything - the property that separates every crackable class in the ladder from every uncrackable one. On 12.6 % of clues the digit is 0: no slice holds two, and the answer is the tray handed back exactly as it came. That is the free format check the whole pool runs in round 1.

WHY THE CLASS WAS REBUILT FROM SCRATCH (v1-v6 were the same rule six times over)
v6 and its five ancestors asked for a CUTTING: the clue was an uncut tray and the answer inserted the knife lines. Under the 4-round / 3-demo format that class went 15, 64 (old 6-round format), 36, 26, 15, 14, 24 % - over fourteen finals it never passed 36 %, and the last three demo-holders scored 26, 14 and 24 %, every one of them having bought the "|" glyph from the demo and none having found the placement. Their words: "insert cuts so each slice holds ~N cells of the header letter, right-to-left greedy - my best rule still misses the reference solver's habit of leaving one blank column at the start of a slice" (durnel1b); "the demo gave 5 cuts for N=3, some slicing through tokens ... cut placement never found" (garrow2a); "a kid would ask how many pieces, and do the cuts go through the cheese?". Three faults, all fatal, all fixed by moving the knife into the clue:
 (1) FIVE CLAUSES, NOT ONE. The old rule was: count slices with >=2 of the named topping; a piece the knife halved counts for BOTH sides; at least 4 slices; every slice at least 3 wide; any cutting that satisfies all of it scores. Clauses 3 and 4 are rejection-only - a demo never shows a violation - and the halves convention is exactly the kind of thing a diff cannot reveal. Measured on v7-shaped trays: a player who has the counting rule exactly right but does not know "the knife never goes through a piece / no slice under 3 wide" produces a legal cutting 4.6 % of the time with 4 cuts, 1.4 % with 5 and 0.4 % with 6. That is the whole of the 14-26 % band the demo-holders lived in.
 (2) THE CAPTION WAS NOT A CHECKSUM. When the answer is a construction, the count cannot falsify anything: whatever a player believes the digit means, some cutting achieves it, so every hypothesis costs a slice of a round instead of costing nothing. That is why v5's near-synonyms measured 77-93 % (they could BUILD to the digit) while the class itself measured 14 %. In v7 the cutting is given, so a wrong reading of the picture is refuted for free on every clue.
 (3) THE ANSWER WAS NOT UNIQUE, so the reference solver needed a tie-break the player could not derive ("the reference answer adds extra cuts I could not derive").

THE THREE DESIGNS THAT WERE REJECTED, WITH THE NUMBERS
 (a) THE KNIFE GOES BETWEEN, NEVER THROUGH - keep the cutting as the answer, forbid cuts through a piece, and drop the halves convention. Rejected: it deletes one clause of five and leaves the two rejection-only ones, which are precisely what the measurement above prices at 0.4-4.6 %. It also keeps the caption as a target rather than a checksum, so v5's 80.6 % row ("slices with exactly two") stays: any wrong reading can still build to the digit.
 (b) ONE CUT - the answer adds exactly one knife line, placed so the left-hand piece holds exactly n of the named topping. Rejected on measurement: on these trays every count from 0 to the number of pieces is reachable by some single cut (7.05 of the 7 possible values on average), so again the digit falsifies nothing offline; and each reachable count has 5.3 legal cut positions on average, so either the class needs a tie-break rule nobody can derive (v1-v6's disease) or the scorer accepts any of them, which makes the rule "a prefix sum" - nameable, and the first thing a model tries.
 (c) THE FENNICK MOVE ON THE SEVERED PIECES - the tray arrives cut, the caption counts the pieces the knife went through, and the answer redraws those pieces split. Rejected: the count is a three-line statistic of the clue and sits inside every player's default sweep (players in this ladder routinely test 19-30 statistics per class), so there is no measurement to discover, and WHICH pieces change is not a question at all - all of them do. The class would be pure rendering: 100 % for whoever buys the demo, 13 % for whoever does not, with no gradient in between and nothing for a kid to contribute.
 (d) CHOSEN - PORTIONS. The tray is cut in the clue and the answer MARKS the slices that hold two or more of the named topping. One clause; the answer is unique, so the demo's diff is the whole rule; the digit becomes a real checksum; and the mark is a sprinkle of stars over the slice's cheese, which is loud in a demo and not guessable from the clue.

WHAT A DEMO SHOWS. Every clue is built from the picture it has to show, so every demo carries the whole sentence and its near-misses. Measured on 500 fresh clues (434 of them cut): a sprinkled slice holding exactly two 100 %; a sprinkled slice holding three ("exactly two" is visibly not the rule) 100 %; a sprinkled slice with its two pieces on ONE row and a second one with its pieces on SEPARATE rows (so neither "two on the same row" nor "it appears in two rows" survives) 100 % each; a plain slice holding ONE piece of it 100 %; a plain slice holding one piece and nothing else at all 100 %; a plain slice holding TWO of ANOTHER topping ("it has to be the named one") 100 %; a slice holding none of it 100 %; the widest slice left plain 100 %.

WITNESS TABLE (500 fresh clues, seeds 100000-100499). Every strategy names the set of slices it would sprinkle and then draws the sprinkle CORRECTLY, so each number is "how often this reading of the picture picks exactly the right slices".
  the rule: a slice with two or more pieces of it        100.00 %
  ...the same rule said in cells: four cells or more     100.00 %   (a restatement)
  ...the same set: the n slices holding most of it       100.00 %   (a restatement)
  the n fullest slices (any topping)                      26.80 %
  the n narrowest slices                                  23.00 %
  n slices at random                                      14.20 %
  nothing sprinkled (the clue handed back)                13.20 %   <- exactly the nought clues
  slices holding EXACTLY two of it                        13.20 %
  slices holding three or more of it                      13.20 %
  slices with two of it on the SAME row                   13.20 %
  slices with it on two different rows                    13.20 %
  the n widest slices                                     13.20 %
  the first n slices                                      13.20 %
  slices with three topping pieces of any mix              0.80 %
  slices with two of ANY one topping                       0.60 %
  slices holding none of it                                0.40 %
  slices holding any of it at all / two pieces of any mix  0.00 %
  slices where it outnumbers every other topping           0.00 %
  every slice sprinkled / the widest slice only            0.00 %
The two 100 % rows below the rule are not rivals but the same set said differently: a player who has either of them has the object, the format and the measurement. Nothing that is a DIFFERENT reading pays more than 26.8 %, and 13.2 % of that is the nought clues, which every strategy that sprinkles nothing collects for free.

THE RENDERING IS WHAT THE DEMO BUYS. The right slices drawn some other way (500 clues): the whole slice starred, toppings and all 13.2 %; starred with "." instead of "*" 13.2 %; toppings upper-cased 13.2 %; toppings rubbed out 13.2 %; one star in the middle of the slice 13.2 %; the slice wiped to blanks 13.2 %; only the first row starred 13.2 % - i.e. all of them score the nought clues and nothing else. So a player who reads the rule off the clues without a demo (the digit is a checksum, so the rule IS findable offline) still has to guess the drawing, and no natural guess pays more than the 13.2 % foothold.

SHAPE AND JUNK ATTACKS (500 clues). Reference 100 %; caption line kept 100 %; crust rows dropped 100 %; trailing spaces 100 %; blank lines inserted 100 %; leading/trailing blank lines 100 % (the house rule about the parameter line holds in both directions). The clue handed back unchanged 13.2 % - exactly the nought clues, where that IS the answer. Knife lines removed 0 %; rows reversed left-right 0 %; a dough row dropped 0 %; a topping moved one cell 0 %; cheese turned to spaces 0 %; the previous clue's answer (demo replay) 0 %; one constant answer for every clue 0 %; empty, whitespace, 4000 characters of junk 0 %. One sprinkled slice left plain 0 %; one plain slice sprinkled as well 3.2 % - those are the cases where the extra slice has no cheese cell in it at all, so the sprinkle is invisible; a slice that IS sprinkled always has cheese, because at most two of its three rows carry pieces.

HOW THE TRAY IS BUILT (generate). The picture is designed and then drawn, which is why every demo teaches. Slice widths first (5-7 slices, each 4-12 columns, tray 34-46 wide, hand-cut: one thin slice and a spread of at least 4). Then the slices are given parts to play: "pair" (two pieces of the named topping side by side on one row), "trio" (three of it, one on each row), optionally "split" (two of it on different rows - the caption then says 3), "lone" (one piece of it and nothing else at all) and "two" (two pieces of ANOTHER topping). The sprinkled parts are only ever given to slices that are not at either end, so the crust never sits inside a sprinkled slice and the drawing question "do the "#" turn into stars?" never arises. The widest slice is never sprinkled. Then a stray piece of the named topping goes into some of the remaining slices (never two, so they stay plain) and 7-11 pieces of the other two toppings are dealt out to the emptiest rows, so that a sprinkled slice is not the fullest one either. Finally look() re-reads the finished tray and refuses it unless every near-miss listed above is actually on the picture. A nought tray is built by the same routine with the sprinkled parts left out, so it looks like every other tray; its named topping has 4-6 pieces where a cut tray's has 6-10, which is visible but worth nothing, since the caption already says 0.

SPEED AND SIZE. generate: mean 0.32 ms, median 0.24, p99 1.03, max 4.95 over 20000 seeds, no empty clue (v6: mean 2.04 ms). solve: mean 0.012 ms, max 0.085 (v6: mean 90 ms - it had to search for a demo; v7 has nothing to search for, because every clue is already the demo). score: mean 0.013 ms, max 0.096 on answers and junk (cap 50). Clue <= 277 chars, solution <= 264. Sources: generate 7395, solve 605, score 306 chars (score cap 512 for picture classes). score(clue, solve(clue)) == 1 on 3000 seeds and on every clue in the tables above. quickcheck --seeds 200: OK, one warning - "score accepts the clue itself as a solution", which on a nought clue is the point of the exercise.

INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH. (1) The clue is a cut tray and the caption says "<letter> <n> sprinkle", so the answer is this picture with something added to n slices; the pool-wide "N verb" probe (hand the picture back unchanged) scores on every "0 sprinkle" clue and on nothing else, which banks 13 % and confirms the format, the letter and what the digit counts. (2) With the cutting given, the digit is testable offline: "slices holding two or more of the letter" comes to the digit on every clue, and a player can confirm it on 70 harvested clues without spending a probe. (3) What is left is the drawing, and that is what the demo buys: the sprinkled slice's cheese - and only the cheese, and only in that slice - turns to stars. (4) One demo settles it, because the same picture also shows a slice with one piece (not sprinkled), a slice with two of another topping (not sprinkled), a sprinkled slice of three, and sprinkled slices whose pieces lie both ways round the rows.

PREDICTION. Two Opus players in a 7-class pool: the one who spends a demo here should crack it in round 2 (one look gives the drawing, and the rule is checkable offline) - 90-100 %; the one who does not should sit at the 13 % foothold unless he guesses the star convention. Predicted mean final 50-60 %, kid score 4.2-4.5 (the object is now a tray of food being served rather than a grid of letters, and the answer is something a kid can point at).

LEVERS. Too easy (the likely direction; the risk is a player who never buys a demo, finds the rule offline from the checksum and then guesses the drawing in a dozen probes): (i) sprinkle only the cheese BETWEEN the two pieces rather than the whole slice - much harder to guess, still one clause, still one look in a demo; (ii) name a topping that is not the commonest one; (iii) count slices holding two or more that also hold nothing else. Too hard (if demo-holders still fail): raise the nought rate, or draw one slice already sprinkled in the clue as a worked instance - the standard "too hard" lever for every picture class in this pool.

def lay(r, lo, u, k):
    """Where k pieces of topping go in one row of a slice u columns wide: every piece is
    two cells and there are at least two cheese cells between pieces."""
    if not k:
        return []
    if 4 * k - 2 > u:
        return None
    b = sorted(r.sample(range(u - 3 * k + 2), k))
    return [lo + b[i] + 3 * i for i in range(k)]


def look(S, x, w):
    """(n, the near-misses this cut tray shows).  n = how many slices hold two or more
    pieces of x.  Each flag is a rival reading of the picture that the picture itself
    refutes, so that the one demo a player pays for can settle it."""
    hot = [sum(d.get(x, (0, 0, 0))) > 1 for d in S]
    f = 0
    for i, d in enumerate(S):
        v = d.get(x, (0, 0, 0))
        t = sum(v)
        other = max([sum(u) for L, u in d.items() if L != x] or [0])
        if t == 1:
            f |= 1                                    # one of it is not enough
            if not other:
                f |= 2                                # and nothing else on that slice
        if t < 2 < other:
            f |= 4                                    # two of ANOTHER topping: not sprinkled
        if hot[i]:
            if t == 2:
                f |= 8                                # a sprinkled slice of exactly two
            else:
                f |= 16                               # and one of three: not "exactly two"
            if max(v) == t:
                f |= 32                               # its pieces all on one row
            elif max(v) < 2:
                f |= 64                               # and one with them on separate rows
        if not t:
            f |= 128                                  # a slice with none of it at all
    if not hot[max(range(len(w)), key=lambda i: w[i])]:
        f |= 256                                      # the widest slice is not sprinkled
    return sum(hot), f


def tray(r, nil):
    """One tray bake, built from the picture it has to show.  The slices are cut first
    and given their parts to play (the sprinkled ones, the one carrying a single piece
    of the named topping, the one carrying two of another topping, the fillers), and the
    toppings are then laid into them."""
    ns = r.randint(5, 7)
    T = r.randint(34, 46)
    w = [4] * ns
    for _ in range(T - 4 * ns):                       # slice widths: hand-cut, never even
        c = [i for i in range(ns) if w[i] < 12]
        if not c:
            return None
        w[r.choice(c)] += 1
    if min(w) > 6 or max(w) - min(w) < 4:
        return None
    u = list(w)
    u[0] -= 2                                         # the crust eats two columns at
    u[-1] -= 2                                        # each end of the tray
    x, y, z = r.sample("mpotacsb", 3)
    plan = [[[] for _ in range(3)] for _ in range(ns)]      # slice -> row -> toppings
    order = sorted(range(ns), key=lambda i: (u[i], r.random()))
    wide = order[-1]                                  # the widest slice is never sprinkled
    mid = [i for i in order if i != wide and 0 < i < ns - 1]
    free = [i for i in order if i != wide and i not in mid]
    r.shuffle(mid)
    r.shuffle(free)
    if nil:
        roles = [("lone", 1), ("two", 1)]             # nothing is sprinkled, so no slice
        for _ in range(r.randint(3, 4)):              # may hold two of the named topping
            roles.append(("one", 1))
    else:
        roles = [("pair", 2), ("trio", 1)]            # the sprinkled slices are never the
        if r.random() < .55:                          # end ones, which carry crust
            roles.append(("split", 2))                # a third one: the caption says 3
        roles += [("lone", 1), ("two", 1)]
    slots = []
    for role, need in roles:
        got = None
        for pool in ((mid,) if role in ("pair", "trio", "split") else (free, mid)):
            for j, i in enumerate(pool):
                if (u[i] + 2) // 4 >= need:
                    got = pool.pop(j)
                    break
            if got is not None:
                break
        if got is None:
            return None
        slots.append((role, got))
    free += mid
    rows = [0, 1, 2]
    lone = None
    for role, i in slots:
        r.shuffle(rows)
        if role == "pair":                            # two of it side by side on one row
            plan[i][rows[0]] += [x, x]
        elif role == "trio":                          # three of it, one on each row
            for q in rows:
                plan[i][q].append(x)
        elif role == "split":                         # two of it, on different rows
            plan[i][rows[0]].append(x)
            plan[i][rows[1]].append(x)
        elif role == "lone":                          # one piece of it and nothing else
            plan[i][rows[0]].append(x)
            lone = i
        elif role == "one":                           # one piece of it among the rest
            plan[i][rows[0]].append(x)
        elif (u[i] + 2) // 4 > 1 and r.random() < .6:  # two of ANOTHER topping, side by
            plan[i][rows[0]] += [y, y]                 # side, and not sprinkled for it
        else:
            plan[i][rows[0]].append(y)
            plan[i][rows[1]].append(y)
    for i in free + [wide]:                           # a stray piece of it here and there
        if r.random() < .45:
            plan[i][r.choice(rows)].append(x)
    for _ in range(r.randint(7, 11)):                 # and the other toppings on top, so
        q = min(rows, key=lambda q: (sum(len(plan[i][q]) for i in range(ns)), r.random()))
        c = [i for i in range(ns)                     # that a sprinkled slice is not the
             if i != lone and 4 * len(plan[i][q]) + 2 <= u[i]]       # fullest one either
        if c:
            plan[r.choice(c)][q].append(r.choice((y, z, z)))
    pos = 0
    cells = [[":"] * T for _ in range(3)]
    for q in range(3):                                # a baked crust two columns thick
        cells[q][0] = cells[q][1] = cells[q][-1] = cells[q][-2] = "#"
    S = [{} for _ in range(ns)]
    cut = []
    for i in range(ns):
        lo = pos + (2 if not i else 0)
        for q in range(3):
            bag = plan[i][q]
            r.shuffle(bag)
            p = lay(r, lo, u[i], len(bag))
            if p is None:
                return None
            for c, L in zip(p, bag):
                cells[q][c] = cells[q][c + 1] = L
                v = S[i].get(L)
                if not v:
                    v = S[i][L] = [0, 0, 0]
                v[q] += 1
        pos += w[i]
        if i < ns - 1:
            cut.append(pos)
    n, f = look(S, x, w)
    if (n == 0) != nil or (not nil and not 2 <= n <= 3) or f & 5 != 5:
        return None
    if not nil and f & 0x1f8 != 0x1f8:      # every cut tray shows the whole sentence
        return None
    crust = "#" * T
    pic = [crust] + ["".join(cs) for cs in cells] + [crust]
    return "%s\n%s %d sprinkle" % (
        "\n".join("".join("|" + ch if i in cut else ch for i, ch in enumerate(l))
                  for l in pic), x, n)


def generate(seed):
    r = random.Random(seed)
    nil = r.random() < 0.12          # ~1 tray in 8 gets no sprinkle at all: the answer
    for _ in range(60):              # is then the clue handed back unchanged
        c = tray(r, nil)
        if c:
            return c
    return ""
solve:
def solve(clue):
  """The tray with every sprinkled slice's cheese turned to stars.  A slice is sprinkled
  when it holds two or more pieces of the caption's topping - a piece is two cells, so
  four cells or more.  The caption line itself is not part of the answer."""
  a = clue.split("\n")
  x = a[-1][0]
  G = [l.split("|") for l in a if ":" in l]
  hot = [sum(g[i].count(x) for g in G) > 3 for i in range(len(G[0]))]
  return "\n".join("|".join(p[i].replace(":", "*") if hot[i] else p[i]
                            for i in range(len(p)))
                   for p in [l.split("|") for l in a[:-1]])
